title: Seabirds racing home over the ocean can get jet-lagged
gist: A Science study led by Oxford's Patrick Lewin used 20 years of GPS tracks (3,688 foraging trips by 1,045 Manx shearwaters) to show that wild seabirds get jet-lagged when flying east or west, skewing their Sun compass in the predicted direction across 335 homing flights. The errors reach about 15 degrees but cost little because birds correct using a map sense; the findings raise questions for bio-inspired autonomous navigation and human jet lag mitigation.

themes.theme: Sun-compass navigation needs an internal clock

insights.claim: Navigating by the Sun requires knowing the time of day, because a heading held constant relative to the ground must shift relative to the Sun from sunrise to sunset; birds rely on a built-in circadian clock for this.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Any Sun-based navigation system, biological or engineered, is only as good as its clock.
insights.quote: Effective navigation by the Sun requires a clock that tells you what time of day it is.

insights.claim: Manx shearwaters recalibrate their internal clock at each dusk and dawn, so for every degree of longitude covered between sunrise and sunset the clock falls four minutes out of sync with local time, making them veer clockwise flying east and anticlockwise flying west.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: East-west travel within a day produces a predictable, quantifiable compass bias.
insights.quote: for every degree of longitude a bird covers between sunrise and sunset, its clock falls four minutes out of sync with local time

insights.claim: Before this study, clock-shift effects on bird navigation had been shown by catching penguins and quickly moving them across longitudes, but not clearly demonstrated in wild animals moving on their own, because the effect is small and needs a lot of data.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Long-running tracking datasets can reveal subtle effects that controlled experiments miss.

themes.theme: Two decades of shearwater GPS tracking

insights.claim: Oxford researchers Tim Guilford and Chris Perrins began GPS-tagging shearwaters in 2004 when the devices became small enough; two decades later the team had tracks from 3,688 foraging trips by 1,045 birds from UK western-coast colonies.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Miniaturized sensors enabled a dataset large enough to detect a small biological effect.

insights.claim: Observed time shifts were tiny, about an hour at most and mostly 10-15 minutes, yet across 335 homing flights out of sight of land the birds veered just as Sun compass predictions said they would.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Even imperceptible clock offsets measurably affect orientation.

insights.claim: Jet-lag-induced navigation errors reached around 15 degrees, but for a shearwater flying 1,000 km east in a day the average error is about seven degrees, adding only about five kilometers if the bird keeps checking its position with its map sense.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Redundant positioning (map sense plus compass) makes compass errors cheap to correct.
insights.quote: If the bird keeps checking where it is, that adds only five kilometers to the trip.

themes.theme: Parallel navigation systems and bio-inspired design

insights.claim: Shearwaters following coastlines still drifted toward or away from shore according to their expected compass error, as clock-shifted homing pigeons do on familiar roads, suggesting birds run compass-based and landmark-based navigation in parallel without fully switching to one.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Biological navigation appears to blend multiple systems continuously rather than switching between them.
